ER training-label sensitivity: strict exclusion versus near-zero treatment

2026-10-30

  • Decision question
  • Design and provenance
  • Training support
  • Common held-out skill
  • Where skill changes
  • Paired CONUS predictions and coverage
  • Interpretation and recommendation

Decision question

Can two training-only ER label treatments reduce negative CONUS respiration predictions while retaining skill on the same physically valid held-out observations and credible coverage, especially in headwaters? The reported comparisons are a sensitivity analysis, not a change to production outputs. A physically valid ER observation is raw StreamMetabolizer ER <= 0; the predicted target is positive respiration magnitude -ER. A prediction of zero is physically nonnegative, but the current downstream workflow requires strictly positive ER, so zero is counted separately and is not usable coverage.

Summary. Both QC variants remove negative predictions throughout the saved CONUS scaling grid while improving common-test R², RMSE, and MAE relative to the unfiltered six-predictor model. B has slightly better pooled skill and retains more training rows than A. Its CONUS ER distribution remains shifted upward from Maavara’s downloaded seven-predictor predictions, particularly in the upper tail. This favors B as the next candidate to validate, while leaving the production choice open.

Design and provenance

The local fits use the archived 70/30 row split (random_state=24) and the same RF settings (500 trees, max_features=5, max_depth=30, max_samples=0.4, oob_score=True, random_state=24). The seven-predictor baseline includes uparea; the other three use the same six predictors without it. A removes raw ER>0 from training. B removes raw ER>0.5 from training and maps raw ER in (0,0.5] to zero respiration magnitude. All four are evaluated on the identical 134,336 original test rows with raw ER<=0. Training and test rows can share sites under this original row split; no site-held-out claim is made.

The Maavara et al. Dryad archive contains the published network predictions and ER notebook. The final seven-predictor notebook cell reports test Pearson r=0.8823235, hence Pearson r²=0.7784948, on its unfiltered test set. It does not give RMSE, MAE, or bias in that cell. Pearson r² is not sklearn R² (r2_score). The published forest’s row-level held-out predictions were not saved locally, so it cannot be scored on the common valid-only test set. Its CONUS predictions are compared on paired network keys below. The Appling et al. source assessment and the earlier wrong-sign audit explain why these training treatments matter.

The source split, retained row counts, and retained sites were checked before fitting; see PREFLIGHT.md. Predictor quantiles show whether A or B materially shrink the range seen during training.

The two sites absent from A’s training set are nwis_09326500 and nwis_09327000; both have low Appling site-minimum confidence. All 154 training rows at the first site and all 113 at the second have raw ER > 0. B also loses the first site; at the second it keeps just three near-zero rows, mapped to zero. Thus B’s one-site advantage should not be interpreted as meaningful retention of measured respiration support at that site.

Interpretation and recommendation

Relative to the unfiltered six-predictor fit, A changes held-out RMSE by -4.45% and B by -4.61%. Across all COMID-months, the unfiltered fit has 152,517 negative predictions and 1,948,815 usable predictions; A has 0 and 2,101,332, and B has 0 and 2,101,332, respectively.

Recommendation: Advance B as the provisional QC candidate for scientific review. It retains 6,251 more training rows than A, has slightly better pooled R²/RMSE/MAE and smaller absolute bias, and provides the same complete positive-prediction coverage. Its extra retained site contributes only three zero-mapped observations, so that site-count difference has little practical value. Both A and B lower RMSE relative to the unfiltered six-predictor fit in every displayed area, flow, season, and region group. The practical difference between A and B is small. Neither establishes agreement with the published seven-predictor CONUS distribution: both retain the elevated upper tail associated with removing uparea, and the monthly median ER is higher than the downloaded Maavara predictions. Before replacing production, decide whether that distribution shift is scientifically credible and consider a site-held-out check, because the original row-wise split shares sites across training and testing. No downstream scripts were rerun.
